title: Silas and the Interior
premise: Ines Reyes, a piano tuner who reads a building's past through its pipes and radiators, lives in their late grandmother's house as a caretaker who never felt entitled to belong. When a late-night radio broadcast airs an unrecorded song written decades ago by Ines's uncle Silas — a man the family erased after he took the blame for a crime committed by someone else — Ines begins tuning the house itself, following its acoustic memory toward the truth. The search forces Ines to confront the surviving family members who arranged their silence around Silas's sacrifice, and to choose between protecting the living and restoring the dead. In the end, Ines testifies to what the house has told them, wins back neither forgiveness nor the house, but finally plays the song in full on the parlor piano, claiming a belonging that no deed can grant or revoke.
about_author: M. M. Fairweather is the pen name of a former building restorer who spent fifteen years listening to old houses before writing about them. They live above a closed music shop and publish rarely.

chapters.title: The Tenant's Key
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Ines tunes a client's piano and returns to the family house they maintain but do not own, cataloguing small signs that the relatives intend to sell. The beat is quiet displacement: Ines knows every sound the house makes but has no legal voice in it.

chapters.title: What the Radiators Remember
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Working alone at night, Ines hears in the heating pipes a rhythmic knocking that matches no mechanical fault — a pattern like song structure. The beat is eerie wonder: the house begins speaking in something older than plumbing.

chapters.title: A Song That Was Never Recorded
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. A late radio program airs an untitled piece; the host says it exists only in manuscript. Ines recognizes it instantly as the melody the radiators have been repeating. The beat is vertigo: private history surfacing in public air.

chapters.title: Silas
chapters.summary: Ines's POV, with remembered fragments from grandmother Rosa. Ines opens the locked trunk and finds sheet music signed by Uncle Silas, the relative no one names, who died young and disgraced. The beat is grief meeting curiosity.

chapters.title: The Family Arrangement
chapters.summary: Alternating POV between Ines and Aunt Marisol. Marisol warns Ines away from the trunk over Sunday dinner while other relatives watch. The beat is polite menace: love enforced as silence.

chapters.title: The Radio Man
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Ines tracks down the broadcaster, Tomás Vega, who received the manuscript anonymously and agrees to share the return address. The beat is cautious alliance: the first person who treats the mystery as worth solving.

chapters.title: House as Witness
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Ines learns to 'tune' the house deliberately, using water pressure, temperature, and pipe resonance to date renovations and find a sealed room behind the parlor wall. The beat is methodical awe turning to dread.

chapters.title: The Sealed Room
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Behind the plaster: a cot, a second manuscript, and letters suggesting Silas lived hidden in the house for months before his arrest. The beat is violation and intimacy at once.

chapters.title: Letters to No One
chapters.summary: Epistolary chapter; Silas's voice via letters, framed by Ines reading aloud. Silas describes composing the song and hints he confessed to protect someone. The beat is tenderness sharpening into suspicion of who he shielded.

chapters.title: Marisol Breaks a Glass
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Confronted gently by Ines, Marisol deflects, then shatters a tumbler and orders Ines out of the house. The beat is guilt wearing anger as armor.

chapters.title: The Deed and the Debt
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. At the county records office Ines discovers the house was nearly forfeited in 1974 until an anonymous payment saved it — the same month Silas was arrested. The beat is cold clarity: money and confession are entangled.

chapters.title: Tomás's Archive
chapters.summary: Tomás's POV. He digs into old court coverage and finds a witness statement that contradicts the official story, plus a photo of Silas with two other young men. The beat is journalistic momentum with a moral undertow.

chapters.title: The Second Name
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Cross-referencing the photo and the payment records, Ines identifies the second man: Uncle Emilio, the beloved patriarch whose heirs now control the estate. The beat is betrayal reorganizing the whole family tree.

chapters.title: What Survival Cost
chapters.summary: Emilio's POV, aged and failing. He remembers the night of the crime, his choice to let Silas take the blame, and the decades of generosity that were really restitution. The beat is self-justification curdling into terror of exposure.

chapters.title: Offer
chapters.summary: Emilio's POV. He summons Ines, offers them the house outright in exchange for the manuscripts and silence. The beat is temptation made concrete: everything Ines lacks, priced at Silas's erasure.

chapters.title: The House Votes
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. That night every pipe in the house sounds at once, the full song running through the walls end to end. Ines understands it as the house refusing the bargain. The beat is uncanny resolve.

chapters.title: Family Council
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs braided: Marisol, cousins, Emilio. The relatives convene to force the sale; Ines arrives with the letters and reads one aloud. The beat is rupture — the arrangement cracking under daylight.

chapters.title: Emilio's Confession
chapters.summary: Emilio's POV. Cornered by his own grandchildren's questions, he confesses to the room, not to the law — a partial justice that satisfies no one fully. The beat is hollow relief.

chapters.title: Running Out of Time
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Emilio suffers a stroke; the sale closes in days; Tomás wants to broadcast the truth. Ines must decide whether justice requires publicity or can live in testimony alone. The beat is compressed urgency.

chapters.title: The Hearing of It
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Ines gives a sworn statement to reopen the record, knowing it may void the estate and leave them homeless. The beat is costly integrity: choosing the truth over shelter.

chapters.title: Sold
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV. The house sells; the family scatters; Marisol, softened, gives Ines Silas's manuscripts and the parlor piano. The beat is loss without bitterness — inheritance redefined as memory.

chapters.title: In Full
chapters.summary: Ines's POV, final scene in the emptied house with the new owners' blessing. Ines tunes the piano and plays Silas's song complete, the radiators answering in resonance. The beat is arrival: belonging claimed through care, not ownership.
